name: Iris Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential. What does a usual building-site day involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am fifty-eight and lead the crew that frames ceilings and fixes timber battens on building sites. My trade certificate and years on the tools mean I can spot an unsafe overhead fixing quickly. I use AI now and then to tidy a materials list after another lead has shown it works, but I still check the ceiling grid. My partner and I have grown children and a few months of expenses saved; I hope to retire at sixty-seven in 2035 if our household income permits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say a quicker batten list is useful as long as nobody skips a pull check overhead. An AI ceiling plan cannot catch a loose fixing above a crowded building corridor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my usual wage and senior role to continue. We have one to six months saved and some similar jobs nearby, though I still need to verify the figures for retiring at sixty-seven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading ceiling work and check sample fixings before any board covers them. I would use the occasional AI list as I do now and review our age-sixty-seven income with my partner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the job in this picture. The retirement calculation is a household task, not a sign that I am leaving early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the pull check for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We test a sample of overhead anchors against the site specification before covering them. A falling ceiling board could hurt someone walking below.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why not learn more AI now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The existing list helper already does the small job I need. I would learn a new control if another crew proved it useful, not for a badge.

say: I would **keep** checking ceiling anchors before boards hide them.
I would **use** the familiar AI list only as a counting aid.
think: My **wage** and lead role look secure, with several months saved.
The **age-sixty-seven** budget still needs checking before an exit decision.
do: **Keep** leading ceiling framing and testing exposed overhead anchors.
**Check** expected age-sixty-seven retirement income against our ordinary housing, food and repair costs with my partner.
S0.quote: An AI ceiling plan cannot catch a loose fixing above a crowded building corridor.
fieldNote: **Iris** uses AI occasionally after proof, while physical overhead safety remains central to her work.
Her **typical** pay, moderate cushion and some local jobs support calm, with retirement still conditional.

steps.text: Keep leading and checking building-site ceiling framing
Review age-sixty-seven retirement figures before deciding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An AI order can arrive early while a ceiling anchor still needs a paid human pull check. I would bring two completed ceiling jobs to our union site meeting and ask for the inspection time in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can imagine the builder shrinking our paid finishing hours if the office plans quicker. My own wages could fall, and a few months of savings would not cover a long cut before retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the ceiling shifts, compare the new schedule with paid hours on two jobs and raise the results at the union meeting. If another crew proves a new AI ordering control prevents missing battens, I would learn it on a real job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about possible paid-hour loss, but I can measure it and act with the crew. I do not reject a useful tool just because I want fair terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which term would you ask the union to secure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paid time to test overhead fixings before boards go up, with the test recorded on the site sheet. I would ask members to put it in the next site agreement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would convince you to learn the new ordering control?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A trusted crew would show that battens and anchors arrived in the right lengths on two jobs. Then I would practice the feature myself on a measured ceiling.

say: I would **take** actual ceiling hours to the union site meeting.
I would **learn** new AI ordering controls after a trusted crew proves them.
think: A **shorter** paid week could drain the cushion before retirement.
**Fair** paid inspection time and useful software can sit together.
do: **Compare** paid ceiling hours on two jobs and raise union site agreement.
**Learn** new AI ordering controls after proof on measured ceilings.
**Keep** paid framing shifts while checking written safety time.
feel: **Anxious** about possible own-hour cuts, with collective options.
S1.quote: An AI order can arrive early while a ceiling anchor still needs a paid human pull check.
fieldNote: She **makes** a specific union meeting request for paid inspection time, not merely a political comment.
Her **steady** adaptability waits for evidence from trusted crews before learning a new AI control.

steps.text: Seek union agreement for paid overhead fixing tests
Learn proven AI ordering control on measured ceiling work
Keep paid ceiling framing while checking terms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew thinking AI reaches plans in 2028 when I am sixty, while hands-on robots arrive around 2031 when I am sixty-three. A robot-fixed ceiling in 2031 still needs someone paid to check the anchors before the boards hide them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my paid ceiling hours could shrink once robots fix standard battens. A few months saved and some nearby jobs give me time to respond, but they do not replace four years of normal pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the builder for a paid supervised trial of robot-fixed ceiling anchors; I would not call it a trial until a place is offered. If a suitable local inspector vacancy is posted with household-covering pay and stop-work authority, and the builder funds a course on paid days, I would enroll and apply after qualifying while keeping paid ceiling shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a real hours risk before retirement, but I have a route to test. No one should sign a covered anchor they have not seen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the trial need to show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A human must inspect sampled anchors against the specification before boards cover them, with authority to stop the installation. I would ask for paid time to do that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the course is offered without a job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not enroll. A fully funded course still needs paid training days and a posted nearby inspector role at a wage that covers our bills.

say: **Thinking** AI changes plans in 2028; robots could fix ceilings around 2031.
I would **request** a paid supervised anchor trial and a real local inspection route.
think: **Four** years of wages may be at risk; savings alone cannot fund that gap.
**Training** needs full funding, paid time, a posted adequate local role and safety authority.
do: **Request** paid supervised robot-ceiling anchor trial with stop-work authority.
**Enrol** in builder-funded paid-time course for posted bill-covering local inspector role with stop-work authority.
**Apply** after qualifying to posted local inspector role with household-covering pay and stop-work authority.
feel: **Anxious** about plausible paid-hour loss, with conditional options.
S2.quote: A robot-fixed ceiling in 2031 still needs someone paid to check the anchors before the boards hide them.
fieldNote: She **requests** a paid trial; no offered place or completed trial is assumed.
**Enrollment** and later application are separate actions, each tied to funding, paid time, a posted local adequate role and safety authority.

steps.text: Keep paid ceiling shifts while requesting supervised paid anchor trial
Enrol in builder-funded paid-time course for posted bill-covering local inspector role with stop-work authority
Apply after qualifying to posted local inspector role with adequate pay and authority

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AI arrives in 2031 when I am sixty-three, with hands-on robots around 2034 when I am sixty-six. A ceiling robot in 2034 could eat the last wage year I meant to use before retiring at sixty-seven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might cover a short loss with savings, but only a real household calculation could say. I would want the builder to keep paying for human anchor checks while I am still on site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading ceiling work and add a new amount from each paid month to our retirement reserve after bills. I would ask the union to seek a written paid-check rule; if robot work cut my shifts, I would apply to posted local ceiling repair jobs only at a wage covering our bills and with safe stop-work authority.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a possible final-year gap, though I have time to build some new cash. The longer lead time lets our crew negotiate before robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you know the reserve actually grew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would mark each new transfer from wages after household bills. The savings we already have would stay counted only once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire at sixty-six to avoid robot work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if verified income covered the extra year and all the years after. Otherwise I would keep earning and search for a posted safe local role.

say: The 2034 **robot** arrival could affect my final paid year before sixty-seven.
I would **seek** a union rule for paid human anchor checks.
think: **Savings** might bridge one year, but retirement needs an income calculation.
**New** money from wages improves the buffer; old cash is not new saving.
do: **Save** new amounts from paid ceiling wages after household bills.
**Seek** union agreement for paid human anchor checks.
**Apply** after robot-hour cuts to posted local repair role with adequate pay and stop-work authority.
feel: **Anxious** about possible final-year wage gap, with time to plan.
S3.quote: A ceiling robot in 2034 could eat the last wage year I meant to use before retiring at sixty-seven.
fieldNote: She **adds** genuinely new savings from pay and takes collective action over paid safety checks.
She does **not** retire at sixty-six on an estimate; the local fallback requires a posted adequate safe role.

steps.text: Save new pay after household bills for retirement buffer
Seek union rule for paid robot-ceiling anchor checks
Apply after cuts to posted local repair role with adequate pay and authority

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew thinking AI arrives in 2036 when I am sixty-eight, and hands-on robots around 2039 when I am seventy-one. A 2039 ceiling robot should not make young carpenters inspect overhead anchors for free.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still care whether the younger carpenters get paid for safety checks. I would not claim I will be on a ceiling crew at seventy-one unless our budget forces a longer working life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep paid ceiling shifts now and verify age-sixty-seven income with my partner. If the figures cover our bills, I would retire at the original 2035 target and remain active at union meetings about paid checks; if not, I would seek posted local ceiling repair work at household-covering pay with safe stop-work authority.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy until our retirement figures are checked, but less exposed to the distant robots. A decade lets younger workers secure terms before machines reach their tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why continue union meetings after retirement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know how much time a safe overhead check takes. Younger members will be the ones doing the work, and I can support their demand for paid time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the household income is short in 2035?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep earning, but only in a posted nearby role with adequate pay and authority to stop unsafe ceiling work. I would not assume a job exists in 2039.

say: The 2036 **thinking** change and 2039 robots may follow my original exit.
I would **keep** supporting paid safety checks for younger carpenters.
think: **Work** after sixty-seven depends on a verified household income shortfall.
**Any** later role needs a real local vacancy, adequate wage and stop-work authority.
do: **Retire** at original 2035 target only if verified household income covers ongoing bills.
**Attend** union meetings for paid robot-ceiling checks after leaving regular site work.
**Apply** if still working to posted local repair role with adequate pay and stop-work authority.
feel: **Uneasy** until the household budget is verified, less worried about distant robots.
S4.quote: A 2039 ceiling robot should not make young carpenters inspect overhead anchors for free.
fieldNote: Her **retirement** target is pre-existing, conditional and earlier than the 2039 physical robot date.
She **remains** active in the union without assuming paid site employment at seventy-one.

steps.text: Retire at original 2035 target only if verified income covers bills
Attend union meetings for paid overhead anchor checks
Apply if working to posted local repair role with adequate pay and stop-work authority

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast case worries me most because robots could cut ceiling wages four years before the retirement I hoped for. A paid trial offer, funded paid-time training and a posted local inspector role at adequate wages would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who has authority to stop a robot-fixed ceiling before the boards go up. I would trust a machine only after the anchors are visible, tested and paid for. A ceiling anchor hidden above a board cannot be inspected by an unpaid promise.

headlineQuote: A ceiling anchor hidden above a board cannot be inspected by an unpaid promise.
portrait: **Iris** is a fifty-eight-year-old trade-certified senior carpenter who leads building-site ceiling framing.
She **has** typical pay, one to six months saved, a partner, grown children and some local jobs.
She **uses** AI occasionally after proof and actively seeks union terms for paid physical checks.
She **hopes** to retire at sixty-seven in 2035 if income permits; later site work requires a budget shortfall.
biggestWorry: **Fast** robots around 2031 could cut paid ceiling work four years before her original retirement target.
whatWouldHelp: An **offered** paid trial, funded paid-time training and a posted local inspector job with adequate wages and stop-work authority would help.
